meta.subject: maths
meta.title: Coordinate Geometry
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 7 (jemh107.pdf, printed pages 99–112)

board_asks: the Distance Formula (length of a side, type of triangle or quadrilateral, collinearity, equidistant points) and the Section Formula for internal division — including the mid-point and the points of trisection. In the rationalised 2026-27 chapter these two formulas carry essentially every mark; area-of-a-triangle by coordinates has been removed from the syllabus.

big_idea.body: Coordinate geometry turns points into number-pairs so that lengths and dividing-points become arithmetic. Two tools do all the work: the Distance Formula gives the length between any two points $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$, and the Section Formula gives the point that splits the segment $AB$ internally in a chosen ratio $m_1 : m_2$ (with the mid-point as the special $1:1$ case). Everything else here — proving a triangle's type, testing whether three points are collinear, finding a missing vertex — is one of these two formulas applied.

definitions.verbatim: So, the distance between the points P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) is PQ = √((x₂ – x₁)² + (y₂ – y₁)²), which is called the distance formula.
definitions.plain: The straight-line distance between two points: square the gap in $x$, square the gap in $y$, add them, take the positive square root — $PQ=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$. The order of subtraction doesn't matter because each difference is squared.

definitions.verbatim: So, the coordinates of the point P(x, y) which divides the line segment joining the points A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂), internally, in the ratio m₁ : m₂ are ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)). This is known as the section formula.
definitions.plain: Where a point lands when it splits the segment from $A$ to $B$ internally in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ — a weighted average of the endpoints. Watch the cross-pattern: the weight $m_1$ (the $PA$ part) multiplies $x_2$, the coordinate of $B$.

definitions.verbatim: Special Case : The mid-point of a line segment divides the line segment in the ratio 1 : 1. Therefore, the coordinates of the mid-point P of the join of the points A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
definitions.plain: Just average the two $x$'s and the two $y$'s — $\left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$. It is the section formula at ratio $1:1$.

definitions.verbatim: The distance of a point from the y-axis is called its x-coordinate, or abscissa.
The distance of a point from the x-axis is called its y-coordinate, or ordinate.
In particular, the distance of a point P(x, y) from the origin O(0, 0) is given by OP = √(x² + y²).

source.note: Remark 1 following the distance formula, p.102

definitions.verbatim: If the ratio in which P divides AB is k : 1, then the coordinates of the point P will be ((kx₂ + x₁)/(k + 1), (ky₂ + y₁)/(k + 1)).

source.note: the single-unknown form used to FIND an unknown ratio

concepts.title: Distance between two points
concepts.body: $PQ=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$ — the length of the segment joining $P(x_1,y_1)$ and $Q(x_2,y_2)$. The distance from the origin is the special case $OP=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Read the two differences straight off the coordinates, then square, add, and take the positive root.
concepts.tested: 2–3 mark “find the distance / length of a side”

concepts.title: The distance formula in disguise — triangles, squares, collinearity
concepts.body: Most questions never say “distance”. To name a triangle, compare its three side-lengths (and check a Pythagoras relation for a right angle); to prove a square, show four equal sides and equal diagonals; to test collinearity, check that the two shorter distances add to the longest ($AB+BC=AC$). All of it is the distance formula, applied a few times.
concepts.tested: prove the type of a triangle / quadrilateral, or show three points are collinear (2–3 marks)

concepts.title: Section formula — internal division
concepts.body: The point $P$ that splits $AB$ internally in the ratio $m_1:m_2$ is $\left(\dfrac{m_1x_2+m_2x_1}{m_1+m_2}, \dfrac{m_1y_2+m_2y_1}{m_1+m_2}\right)$. The weights cross over — $m_1$ multiplies the coordinates of $B$. In the rationalised syllabus only internal division is examined; external division is left for higher classes.
concepts.tested: find the dividing point, or the ratio — including case-study setups (2–3 marks)

concepts.title: Mid-point & points of trisection
concepts.body: The mid-point is just the average of the coordinates: $\left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$. The two points of trisection split $AB$ into three equal parts — apply the section formula at ratios $1:2$ and $2:1$. A common exam use: a missing vertex of a parallelogram, since its diagonals bisect each other (equal mid-points).
concepts.tested: mid-point, points of trisection, or the missing vertex of a parallelogram

concepts.title: Working backwards — find a ratio or a coordinate
concepts.body: When the ratio is unknown, assume it is $k:1$, apply the section formula, and solve the coordinate you already know. A point on the $y$-axis has $x=0$; a point on the $x$-axis has $y=0$ — that single fact becomes the equation you solve. Equidistant conditions ($AP=BP$) square to a neat linear relation between $x$ and $y$.
concepts.tested: “in what ratio does the y-axis divide…”, find $k$, or an equidistant-point relation

examples.shape: Distance formula → type of triangle · NCERT Example 1
examples.problem_verbatim: Do the points (3, 2), (–2, –3) and (2, 3) form a triangle? If so, name the type of triangle formed.

solution_steps.lead: Apply the distance formula to all three pairs.

solution_steps.text: The sum of any two of these distances is greater than the third, so $P$, $Q$, $R$ form a triangle.
$PQ^2+PR^2=50+2=52=QR^2$, so by the converse of the Pythagoras theorem $\angle P=90°$ — it is a right triangle.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1½ for the three side-lengths via the distance formula, ½ for the triangle-inequality conclusion, 1 for naming it a right triangle by the converse of Pythagoras ($PQ^2+PR^2=QR^2$).

source.note: problem + first distances on p.102; right-angle conclusion at top of p.103

examples.problem_verbatim: Fig. 7.6 shows the arrangement of desks in a classroom. Ashima, Bharti and Camella are seated at A(3, 1), B(6, 4) and C(8, 6) respectively. Do you think they are seated in a line? Give reasons for your answer.

solution_steps.text: $AB+BC=3\sqrt2+2\sqrt2=5\sqrt2=AC$, so $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear — they are seated in a line.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape: 1 for the three distances, 1 for the collinearity conclusion $AB+BC=AC$. No area calculation is needed — the distance test alone settles whether the points lie on one line.

source.note: problem (with Fig. 7.6) on p.103; solution on p.104

examples.shape: Equidistant point on the y-axis · NCERT Example 5
examples.problem_verbatim: Find a point on the y-axis which is equidistant from the points A(6, 5) and B(– 4, 3).

solution_steps.lead: A point on the y-axis is $(0, y)$.
solution_steps.text: Let $P(0,y)$ be equidistant from $A(6,5)$ and $B(-4,3)$, so $AP^2=BP^2$.
solution_steps.concept_tag: point on an axis has x = 0

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for using the form $(0, y)$ and setting $AP^2=BP^2$, 1 for the expanded equation, 1 for solving to $y=9$ and stating the point $(0, 9)$.

source.note: problem on p.104; solution completes on p.105

examples.problem_verbatim: Find the coordinates of the point which divides the line segment joining the points (4, – 3) and (8, 5) in the ratio 3 : 1 internally.
examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape: ½ for the correct section-formula set-up, ½ + ½ for the x- and y-coordinates, ½ for stating the point $(7, 3)$.

examples.problem_verbatim: Find the coordinates of the points of trisection (i.e., points dividing in three equal parts) of the line segment joining the points A(2, – 2) and B(– 7, 4).

solution_steps.lead: P is the first trisection point — ratio 1 : 2.

solution_steps.text: The points of trisection are $(-1, 0)$ and $(-4, 2)$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for $P$ at ratio $1:2$, 1 for $Q$ at ratio $2:1$, 1 for stating both trisection points. Applying the section formula twice — not the mid-point — is the key.

strategies.cue: Need a length or the type of a shape?
strategies.text: Distance formula on every relevant pair, then compare. Equal sides, equal diagonals, or a Pythagoras relation names the figure.
Compute the three distances; if the two smaller ones sum to the largest, the points are collinear — no area needed.

strategies.cue: Split a segment in a ratio?
strategies.text: Section formula. Keep the weights straight: $m_1$ pairs with the FAR point (the cross pattern).
Mid-point = average the coordinates. Trisection = section formula at $1:2$ and again at $2:1$.
Assume the ratio is $k:1$, apply the section formula, and use the coordinate you know — $0$ on an axis — as the equation to solve.

pitfalls.text: Swapping the section-formula weights — writing $m_1x_1$ instead of $m_1x_2$. The ratio's first part multiplies the SECOND point's coordinate.
Sign slips with negative coordinates — $(x_2-x_1)$ with $x_1$ negative becomes a sum, e.g. $3-(-2)=5$, not $1$.
Dropping the square root, or taking the negative root — distance is always the positive square root.
Forgetting the axis condition — a point on the $y$-axis has $x=0$ (on the $x$-axis, $y=0$); that is the equation you solve for the ratio or the point.

third_tab_content.name: The Distance Formula — straight from Pythagoras
third_tab_content.intro: NCERT builds the distance formula on p.102 by dropping perpendiculars to the x-axis and reading off a right triangle (Fig. 7.5). The two legs come directly from the coordinates, and one application of the Pythagoras theorem gives the length — this is exactly why the formula has that squared-differences shape.

steps.claim: Set up the two points and drop perpendiculars.
steps.justification: Draw PR and QS perpendicular to the x-axis; a perpendicular from P meets QS at T (NCERT Fig. 7.5).

steps.claim: Read the horizontal leg from the x-coordinates.
Read the vertical leg from the y-coordinates.
Apply the Pythagoras theorem in right triangle PTQ.
Take the positive square root — distance is non-negative.

source.note: derivation via the Fig. 7.5 construction, p.102

fig_distance_plane.caption: The distance between P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the coordinate differences.
fig_distance_plane.legend: Horizontal leg = x₂ − x₁, vertical leg = y₂ − y₁; PQ = √(sum of their squares).

fig_section_divide.caption: P divides AB internally in the ratio m₁ : m₂ — shown for A(4, −3), B(8, 5), ratio 3 : 1, giving P(7, 3).
fig_section_divide.legend: P lies on segment AB with AP : PB = m₁ : m₂; its coordinates are the weighted average of A and B.
